To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) instructors who design their courses in ways consistent with existing definitions of good practice are associated with higher student engagement and academic achievement, and that (2) this relationship is mediated by the instructor's use of the learning management system (i.e., LMS), which is consistent with the idea of LMS course design as a variable in a learning analytics intervention.

(a) the LMS course design variables we have identified are significantly associated with both engagement and performance; (b) these associations hold across different disciplines; (c) the variables we identified can be operationalized and used to identify courses with the most potential for improvement, and (d) there is significant variation in the degree to which instructors use the variables.

(a) LMS course design is an effective variable to predict academic performance; (b) LMS course redesign may be one of most scalable forms of intervention an institution can pursue; and (c) faculty development is a critical factor in the successful redesign of LMS courses.
